Subject: Recommendation for a Building Survey on Your 1930s Semi

Dear [Recipient],

I hope this email finds you well. I understand that you're considering purchasing a 1930s semi, which appears to be well-maintained, but I wanted to bring to your attention the importance of conducting a full structural (building) survey.

While the property may seem sound, loft alterations can often hide structural changes that may not be immediately apparent. In such cases, a full survey would offer more reassurance, particularly if you're planning future works or renovations. This type of survey would provide a comprehensive assessment of the property's condition, identifying any potential issues that could impact its value or your enjoyment of the property.

I'd be happy to recommend a local surveyor who has extensive experience with similar properties. They have a proven track record of providing detailed and insightful reports, helping buyers make informed decisions.

Would you like me to pass on their contact details? Please let me know, and I'll be happy to facilitate an introduction.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

task_details: Buyer: couple seeking value, viewed a 3-bed mid-terrace in Enfield Town, guide price £525,000. Viewing notes: house in good condition but recent comparable sales in same street sold at £495k and £505k in last three months, EPC C. Buyer reaction: felt asking price was optimistic.
personalized: Hi there, lovely to meet you at the mid-terrace in Enfield Town today. The property is in nice condition and the rooms flow well. I wanted to flag that recent comparable sales on the same street have completed at around £495,000 and £505,000 in the last three months, so the guide price of £525,000 is a touch above recent market levels. EPC is C. If you’re interested, I’d suggest one of two approaches: make a cautious offer in line with the recent comps and be prepared to move up during negotiation, or, if you think the house is worth the premium for other reasons, make a stronger initial offer but ask for appliances or completion flexibility in return. I can prepare a short comparative market note for you to use during offer discussions. Want me to do that? Best, Aisha

  - Option A: make a cautious offer in line with recent comparable sales and be prepared to increase the offer during negotiation.

Dear [Recipient],

I wanted to take a moment to thank you for taking the time to view the flat in the converted Victorian house. I understand that you're working to a tight budget, and I appreciate your interest in the property.

As we discussed, I wanted to provide you with some key facts about the flat. The property is a tidy conversion with interior works that have been well done. The council tax band is D, which comes to approximately £2,100 per year. Additionally, there is a service charge of around £900 per year, which covers the costs associated with maintaining the building.

The flat is available on a 98-year lease, and its EPC rating is C. I understand that these costs can add up, and I want to make sure you have a clear understanding of what you're committing to.

If you'd like, I'd be happy to prepare a full monthly cost breakdown for you, covering the mortgage, council tax, service charge, and utilities. This will give you a better idea of the overall costs involved.

Please let me know if you'd like me to prepare this breakdown, and I'll get it sent over to you as soon as possible.

Best regards,
Aisha

Subject: Follow-up on Duplex Viewing in Enfield

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to follow up on our viewing of the duplex in Enfield today. As we discussed, I completely agree that the interior finish is great and the space feels modern and light.

Could you please let me know which option you prefer? I'm looking forward to hearing back from you and moving forward with your property search.

Best regards,
Aisha

task_instruction: Write a positive but realistic follow-up after a second viewing suggesting making an offer
task_details: Buyer: couple who returned for a second viewing and expressed clear interest. Property: 3-bed semi with modern kitchen, garden, within local school catchment, EPC B, guide price offers over £540,000. Viewing notes: second viewing confirmed initial positive impression; buyer asked about typical negotiation margin. Buyer reaction: keen to proceed but unsure what to offer.
personalized: Hiya, lovely to see you again today and glad the second viewing confirmed your first impressions. The modern kitchen and garden are very desirable, and being in the local school catchment is an added bonus. EPC is B and the seller has set offers over £540,000. Given current local activity on similar homes, a sensible starting point would be to offer slightly below the guide with a clear timeline for exchange to show you’re serious. If you want I can prepare a suggested offer letter and explain how to position your offer to be competitive without overpaying. If you’re happy, tell me the figure you’re considering and I’ll put it forward and manage the negotiation. Best wishes, Aisha
prompt:
Write a email

- Objectives:
  - Confirm the recipient remains interested after the second viewing.
  - Propose next steps to make an offer (including preparing a suggested offer letter and explaining how to position the offer).
  - Recommend offering slightly below the seller’s guide price with a clear timeline for exchange to demonstrate seriousness.
  - Ask the recipient to provide the figure they want to offer.
  - Confirm that Aisha will submit the offer and manage the negotiation if instructed.

- Factual information to include:
  - Property features: modern kitchen and garden.

Subject: Next Steps for Making an Offer on [Property Address]

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to follow up on your second viewing of [Property Address] to confirm whether you remain interested in making an offer. As you may recall, this beautiful property boasts a modern kitchen, a lovely garden, and is located within the local school catchment area, making it an ideal choice for families.

The EPC rating for the property is B, and after careful consideration, we believe it has the potential to be a fantastic long-term investment. Given the seller's guidance of £540,000, we would like to propose a strategy of making an offer slightly below this figure to demonstrate our seriousness and flexibility.

To move forward, we would like to request that you provide us with a figure that you would be comfortable offering for the property. Once we have this information, Aisha will prepare a suggested offer letter and explain how to position the offer competitively without overpaying.

task_details: Buyer: eco-conscious couple. Property: 3-bed mid-terrace with single-glazed windows, older gas boiler, EPC E, guide price £430,000. Viewing notes: property needs insulation and window upgrades; buyer asked about likely energy improvements and grants. Buyer reaction: interested but wanted to estimate cost and savings.
personalized: Hi there, thanks for viewing the mid-terrace today. I know energy performance matters to you — the house currently has single-glazed windows and an older boiler, hence the EPC rating of E. There’s good scope to improve insulation, replace windows and upgrade the boiler which would significantly reduce running costs and improve comfort. There are currently government schemes and local grants that sometimes help with insulation and boiler replacements; I can pull together likely costs and possible funding options for you. If you’d like, I can also arrange a home energy assessor to provide a targeted estimate of improvements and expected savings. Want me to set that up? Warmly, Aisha

task_details: Seller’s Victorian two-bed cottage in Grange Park listed at £385,000. Buyer offers £370,000 but asks seller to carry out all repairs identified in survey (roof and damp), estimated at £10k. Recent comps support original asking. Seller prefers to leave property as-is. personalized:
Hi John,

Thanks for sending through the buyer’s terms. They’ve put in an offer of £370,000 and asked that we carry out repairs totalling about £10,000 following their survey. Based on recent comps for similar period cottages in Grange Park, your guide price of £385,000 remains realistic.

We propose a compromise: counter at £378,000 with the property sold as seen. That gives the buyer a reduction to cover the repairs but keeps you out of the work. If they accept £378,000, we can agree a 28-day exchange to keep the sale moving and request a slightly larger deposit to show commitment.

If you’d prefer to do one small, high-impact repair (for example a new ridge tile) we can offer £382,000 instead. Give me a bell and we’ll choose the best route.

All the best, 
Aisha

task_instruction: Advise seller on handling a gazumping situation with competing offers
task_details: Seller accepted a £540,000 offer on a semi in Edmonton but a new buyer has since offered £560,000. The initial buyer is part-way through surveys. Seller feels torn. Provide an email advising on ethics, legal position, and recommending a course of action that protects seller but maintains relationships.
personalized:
Hi David,

I know this is a tricky one — you had a firm agreement at £540,000 and now a higher bid of £560,000 has come in. Legally, until contracts are exchanged the sale isn’t binding, but pulling out of a verbal or informal agreement can damage relationships and your reputation locally.

My recommendation is to contact the first buyer’s solicitor immediately to establish their timetable and push for exchange. Tell the second buyer we’re open to a higher offer but only if they can match the timetable and provide a larger deposit and proof of funds. Based on recent comps in Edmonton, £560,000 is attractive, but we should be transparent and aim to exchange quickly to avoid further complications.

If you want, I’ll handle the communications and aim to secure the best outcome without burning bridges.

Best, 
Aisha

Give me a bell if you’d like to proceed and I’ll confirm with the buyer.

All the best, 
Aisha

If you’re happy with that number, I’ll send the counter now.

Best regards, 
Aisha

We’ve received a £495,000 offer on your three-bed, but it’s subject to the buyer selling their own property with no clear timeframe. That’s riskier than a mortgage-condition offer.

We propose accepting the conditional offer only if the buyer provides a non-refundable reservation fee of 2% and commits to a maximum 12-week chain-free timescale with monthly progress updates. This gives you some security and compensates for the uncertainty. If they won’t agree, I’d recommend keeping marketing live.

Happy to discuss the precise wording for the reservation agreement.

Warmly, 
Aisha

task_instruction: Negotiate an offer when buyer requests seller to contribute to stamp duty
task_details: Buyer offers £455,000 on a mid-terrace in Grange Park asking £465,000 but asks seller to contribute £5,000 towards their stamp duty costs. Seller is reluctant to pay buyer costs. Draft an assertive email proposing an alternative — lower price or no contribution — with justification.
personalized:
Hi Michelle,

Buyer has offered £455,000 but asked you to contribute £5,000 toward their stamp duty. It’s unusual for sellers to cover buyers’ transfer taxes and it would effectively reduce your net by that amount.

We propose two alternatives: keep your asking position and counter at £462,000 with no contribution, or accept the £455,000 only if the buyer increases their deposit to 10% to show commitment. Based on recent comps in Grange Park, holding firm on net proceeds is reasonable.

Which option do you prefer? I’ll respond accordingly.

Best wishes, 
Aisha

Aisha

I’ll speak to their solicitor and see what they can commit to.

Aisha

task_instruction: Advise seller about accepting an offer subject to banks valuation shortfall
task_details: Buyer has offered £602,000 on a five-bed in Cockfosters, subject to a bank valuation and potential valuation shortfall. Seller worries about renegotiation. Draft an email recommending a clause: buyer to guarantee they will cover a shortfall up to a set amount or seller will be free to re-market.
personalized:
Hi Zahra,

Offer of £602,000 is solid but it’s subject to bank valuation which sometimes comes in under purchase price. To avoid post-survey renegotiation, we should get the buyer to commit in writing.

We propose accepting the offer only if the buyer guarantees to cover any valuation shortfall up to £10,000 or accepts that if the shortfall is larger, you are free to re-market. This protects you from being forced into a reduced price at a late stage.

I’ll draft the wording for the solicitor to include in the memorandum of sale if you’re happy.

Warm regards, 
Aisha

- Proposed terms to include in buyer’s commitment:
  - buyer guarantees to cover any valuation shortfall up to £10,000
  - if the valuation shortfall exceeds £10,000, Zahra may re-market the property (i.e., is free to withdraw and seek other buyers)

task_details: Buyer wants the seller to remove an older garden shed. Seller is happy to leave it but wants a higher price. Property is a three-bed in Winchmore Hill asking £575,000. Hi Nadine,

The buyer’s at £570,000 but asked for the garden shed to be removed. You’re happy to leave it in place, which is often not a major issue for buyers.

We propose asking the buyer to increase to £573,000 if you leave the shed. That small uplift compensates you for keeping the item without having to organise removal. If they insist on removal, we can offer it for a lower price or ask them to contribute to costs.

Let me know which you prefer and I’ll get back to the buyer.

Best, 
Aisha

task_instruction: Advise seller to accept a lower offer in exchange for buyer taking a leasehold extension responsibility
task_details: Seller has a leasehold flat in Grange Park with 82 years remaining, guide £290,000. Buyer offers £285,000 but asks seller to extend the lease before completion. personalized:
Hi Yasmin,

Buyer’s offered £285,000 but wants you to undertake a lease extension before completion. Extending the lease is time-consuming and costly for you.

We propose accepting £285,000 on condition that the buyer undertakes the lease extension after completion at their cost and provides a timescale and solicitor undertaking. That way you avoid the upfront work and the buyer takes on the responsibility they asked for. If they won’t agree, we should hold out for a higher offer or do the extension ourselves, but I’d recommend the first route.

Happy to negotiate the wording with their solicitor.

Kind regards, 
Aisha

task_instruction: Recommend a small price reduction to meet survey concerns quickly
task_details: Buyer offered £525,000 on a semi in Enfield but survey flagged minor subsidence concerns needing specialist costs estimated at £7,000. Buyer asks seller to pay. Seller prefers to reduce price. Draft an email proposing a price reduction of £6,000 and keep sale on track.

Hi Peter,

The buyer’s survey has flagged minor subsidence concerns estimated at about £7,000 and they’re asking you to cover the cost. To keep the sale moving and avoid delays, a price reduction is the pragmatic route.

We propose reducing the price by £6,000 to £519,000 and selling as seen. That compensates the buyer substantially while avoiding you having to organise, pay for, and delay remedial work. Based on recent local cases, buyers accept this approach when the adjustment is fair.

If you’re agreeable, I’ll put the counter forward today.

Warmly, 
Aisha

task_instruction: Advise seller to accept a slightly lower offer if buyer removes onward chain condition
task_details: Buyer offers £470,000 for a three-bed on Ponders End Road but is subject to sale of another property. Buyer can, however, proceed if they secure a bridging loan. Seller prefers chain-free buyers. Draft an email recommending acceptance at £468,000 if the buyer confirms bridging loan and quicker exchange.
personalized:
Hi Rachael,

We have a conditional offer of £470,000 but the buyer is dependent on selling their property. They’ve said they could use a bridging loan to proceed chain-free.

We propose accepting £468,000 if they confirm, in writing, that they will proceed with a bridging loan and commit to a 28-day exchange. That gives you a near-chain-free sale and slightly better security than waiting for their own sale, while only a small concession on price.

If that sounds good, I’ll ask for the lender’s details and timeline.

Best wishes, 
Aisha

task_details: Seller with two children selling a three-bed in Enfield wants to complete during school holidays. Buyer offers guide price £495,000 but requests a mid-term completion. The buyer has offered the full £495,000 but wants a mid-term completion which doesn’t suit your family plans. You’d prefer to complete during the school holidays.

We propose accepting the offer on the condition that the buyer either agrees to a completion date that falls within the upcoming school holidays or contributes up to £1,200 towards short-term accommodation costs if a mid-term completion is unavoidable. That balances the buyer’s timeline with your family needs and keeps the sale moving.

Tell me which option you prefer and I’ll set it out to the buyer.

Warm regards, 
Aisha

Hiya Sam,

Lovely news again on the offer being accepted for 12 Oak Walk. First, congrats — and next, a quick clear plan so you know what happens now.

First, within 48 hours please instruct your conveyancer and send me their contact details so I can tell the seller’s solicitor. Your conveyancer will open your file and start searches. Next, you’ll need to get your mortgage valuation arranged; that usually happens within 5 working days of your lender receiving instruction. I’ll confirm the postcode and send over the sales particulars to speed that up.

Then we’ll arrange a full homebuyer’s survey if you want one. I’d suggest organising that within the next 7–10 days. Your surveyor will book a time with you directly; let me know what suits and I can pop round on the day if you want.

You’ll also need to prepare the deposit for exchange. Your conveyancer will tell you the exact sum, but aim to have proof of funds ready within two weeks. Meanwhile the solicitors will draft the contract and raise enquiries. Give those a prompt response so we keep to the timetable.

Our provisional target is exchange in about eight weeks and completion two weeks after exchange. I’ll chase the chain weekly and update you if anything changes. If you need me to liaise with your lender or conveyancer I’m happy to do that.

Give me a bell if you want to talk it through. I can pop into Grange Park to meet your solicitor if that helps.

All the best,
Aisha

Give me a bell if you want to talk through the tenant side. I can pop in to the property to meet the tenants if that helps reassure them and keep the sale moving.

Best wishes,
Aisha

Nice one on 5 Manor Court. Since this is a buy-to-let there are a few landlord-specific steps to get right.

I can recommend trusted local clerks who handle inventories and meter readings.

We’ll aim to exchange in about six weeks, subject to the mortgage offer and searches. I’ll chase weekly and keep you updated.

Give me a bell if you want me to recommend a landlord solicitor or local HMO advice. I’m happy to help sort the practical side.

All the best,
Aisha

Cheers,
Aisha

Aisha

personalized:
Hiya everyone,

Thanks for getting everything to this stage. We’re in a four-way chain and everyone’s keen to keep the momentum. Here’s how I’ll coordinate things and what you can expect.

First, I’ll set provisional exchange and completion dates for each link and circulate them to all solicitors this week. Next, I’ll run weekly progress calls with solicitors and update the chain every Monday so we spot any issues early. If any link stalls we’ll look at contingency options such as short completions staggered to release funds, or temporary accommodation for buyers who need a little extra time.

Please make sure your conveyancers respond promptly to enquiries and that buyers have funds and mortgage conditions ready. If anyone expects a delay tell me straight away so I can rework the timeline. I’ll also prepare a clear completion day timeline when exchange is near so keys and funds are coordinated.

Give me a bell if you want to go through contingency options or need help arranging short-term storage or removals locally.

All the best,
Aisha

task_details: Buyer and seller will conduct a pre-completion inspection day of completion. personalized:
Hiya both,

With completion day approaching, here’s how we’ll handle the pre-completion inspection and key handover so it goes smoothly.

First, the buyer or their representative should conduct a pre-completion inspection on the morning of completion to confirm the property’s condition and that agreed fixtures are in place. Check meter readings, confirm that all keys and remote controls are present and note any last-minute issues. The seller should make sure the property is vacated to the agreed condition and leave any manuals or warranties.

Keys are usually released once the seller’s solicitor confirms the completion monies have cleared and the register is updated. We’ll agree a completion time in advance — I suggest a time mid-afternoon to allow banks to process the transfers. I’ll confirm with both solicitors the exact timing the day before.

Give me a bell if you’d like me to attend the inspection. I can meet you at the property and help go through the checklist.

Warmly,
Aisha

task_instruction: Landlord selling with tenants needing notice or transfer arrangements
task_details: Landlord Marcus is selling a property with tenants present and needs to either obtain vacant possession or transfer the tenancy to the buyer. Explain steps including giving tenant notice if required, solicitor coordination, deposit transfer details, and timelines. Clarify responsibilities and offer to liaise with tenants.
personalized:
Hiya Marcus,

Thanks — selling with tenants in place is common and we’ll make sure it’s handled properly. First, confirm whether you and the buyer have agreed on vacant possession or that the tenancy will transfer on completion. If vacant possession is required your solicitor will advise on the correct notice period and paperwork. If the tenancy transfers, your solicitor must provide deposit protection details and the AST so the buyer’s solicitor can record the tenancy.

Next, please ensure the tenant’s deposit protection certificate and contact details are provided to the buyer’s solicitor before exchange. Your solicitor will coordinate the legal transfer of the AST or prepare the paperwork for a vacate notice. Timelines vary, but allow at least two to four weeks to serve notices and provide the necessary documentation.

If you’d like, I can speak with the tenants to reassure them and explain the process. Give me a bell and I’ll arrange a suitable time to visit.

Best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explaining mortgage offer conditions and outstanding documents
task_details: Buyer Pri accepted offer but lender has conditions: proof of additional income, updated bank statements, employer letter, and ID checks within 14 days. Provide a checklist of what to send, who handles it, and timeline to avoid delaying exchange. Keep tone reassuring and practical.
personalized:
Hiya Pri,

Good progress on your offer. Your lender has issued a mortgage offer with a few standard conditions we need to satisfy quickly so it doesn’t hold up exchange.

First, please provide updated bank statements for the last three months, a written employer confirmation of your income (or your latest payslip) and any additional proof of funds for your deposit. Also make sure your ID documents are up to date and with your broker or solicitor for verification. Aim to get these to your mortgage broker or lender within 14 days so the valuation and final paperwork can proceed.

Your broker can upload documents directly to the lender portal; if you want me to nudge them or call the lender on your behalf I’m happy to help. Once the lender confirms the conditions are cleared we can move towards exchange.

Give me a bell if you want me to check the exact wording of the conditions with your broker. I’ll keep it straightforward and chase as needed.

Cheers,
Aisha

Thanks — I’ve noted you need the building regulation completion certificates and the planning permission documents for the rear extension. These are important for conveyancing, insurance and any future works.

First, please ask the seller to provide the original certificates or solicitor-certified copies within 7 days. If there’s any delay obtaining the certificates we can consider indemnity insurance as a workaround, but it’s best to have the official documents where possible. I’ll chase the seller and their solicitor to prioritise this so we don’t delay your timeline.

Give me a bell if you want me to contact the seller’s solicitor directly and push for the documents.

Kind regards,
Aisha

All the best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Guidance on stamp duty payment and solicitor responsibilities
task_details: Buyer Leila needs clarity on stamp duty land tax (SDLT). Explain that the buyer pays SDLT via their solicitor, the typical deadline (usually within 14 or 30 days depending on jurisdiction), how much is due approximately based on purchase price £525,000, and that solicitor will coordinate payment but funds must be available. Keep it informative and reassuring and include next steps.
personalized:
Hiya Leila,

Just to cover stamp duty for your purchase at £525,000 — your solicitor will arrange payment but you’ll need to have the funds available at completion. The solicitor calculates the exact tax, submits the return and pays the SDLT to HMRC on your behalf and confirms it when done.

Typically the payment is handled shortly after completion and your solicitor will let you know the exact figure in advance. It’s a good idea to have the estimated amount ready with your completion funds so nothing delays the final transfer. If you’d like, I can ask your solicitor for an estimated SDLT figure today so you know what to expect.

Give me a bell if you want me to request that estimate or explain how the solicitor handles the payment. Happy to help keep it simple.

Best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Changing conveyancer request after offer acceptance
task_details: Buyer James wants to change solicitors after offer accepted. Outline the steps: notify current conveyancer, instruct new one, transfer of files, potential delays, costs, and advise informing agent and seller's solicitor. Provide recommended timeline to minimize delays and offer support to liaise.
personalized:
Hiya James,

No problem about changing conveyancers — it happens. First, formally instruct your new solicitor and ask them to write to your current conveyancer requesting the file transfer. Second, let me and the seller’s solicitor know you’re changing so we don’t miss any deadlines.

There can be a small delay while records transfer, often a week or so. Ask your new solicitor to request the earlier paperwork and chase for any outstanding searches or enquiries. There may be a small administrative charge for handling the transfer; check that with both firms. Aim to have the new solicitor fully instructed within 48–72 hours to keep the process moving.

If you like I’ll contact the seller’s solicitor and let them know you’ve appointed a new conveyancer. Give me a bell and I’ll make the call.

Cheers,
Aisha

Best,
Aisha

task_details: After a homebuyer survey reported damp in the cellar and some roof tiles loose, buyer wants to negotiate. Hiya,

Thanks for sending the survey report. The damp in the cellar and the loose roof tiles are things we can work with. Here are sensible options and how we’ll approach them.

First, we can ask the seller to carry out the repairs before exchange. That means getting a quote and setting a deadline for the work to be done and signed off. Second, we can ask for a price reduction or a completion-day contribution to cover the remedial costs; we’d need a couple of quotes to back up the amount. Third, if the works are minor you may accept them and have your builder do them after completion with a reduced price.

If you’d like me to, I can request two local tradespeople to provide quotes within 5–7 days so we have firm numbers to negotiate with the seller. Tell me which option you prefer and I’ll take it from there.

Give me a bell and we’ll decide the best route together.

Warmly,
Aisha

task_instruction: Advice on lease extension process where lease below 80 years
task_details: Buyer Oliver is buying a flat where the lease is 78 years. Explain implications for mortgages and resale, steps to instruct a specialist solicitor and surveyor, estimated timeframe and costs for a statutory lease extension, and whether to proceed before or after purchase. Provide clear next steps and offer recommendations.
personalized:
Hiya Oliver,

A lease under 80 years is important to flag. Lenders can be cautious and extending later can be more expensive, so it’s good to consider the options now.

First, get a specialist leasehold solicitor and a chartered surveyor to estimate the premium and likely legal costs for a statutory lease extension. Your solicitor will calculate the compensation owed to the freeholder and the surveyor will value the premium. The statutory process typically takes several months once started and can cost a few thousand pounds depending on the property and the remaining years.

You can choose to buy now and extend later, or negotiate for the seller to start the extension before exchange. If you plan to mortgage, check with your lender — some will lend with a lease under 80 years but may ask for a plan for extension. I can recommend local leasehold specialists who handle Enfield flats regularly.

Give me a bell if you want those recommendations or if you’d like me to ask the seller to start the extension process before exchange.

Best wishes,
Aisha

Hiya Eva,

Good to see the mortgage valuation is moving. Just to explain quickly: a mortgage valuation is for the lender to check the property’s value and their security. It’s not a detailed look at condition. A full homebuyer’s survey or a building survey gives you a proper picture of the property’s condition and any issues that could cost money down the line.

Given this is a mid-19th century terrace with some age-related work likely, I’d recommend getting a full building survey. It usually takes a couple of hours on site and a week for the written report. It does cost more than a valuation but is well worth it for older properties. Arrange the survey quickly — within the next 7–10 days — so you have time to act on any findings before exchange.

I’ve got a couple of local surveyors who specialise in period houses; give me a bell and I’ll pass their details over and book one for you.

Best,
Aisha

Request solicitor to commence possession proceedings under Grounds 8 and discretionary grounds, provide list of documents enclosed (tenancy agreement, rent statement, correspondence, witness statements) and request estimate of costs and timeline. Signed by Aisha Campbell as instructing agent.
personalized: This is to formally instruct you to commence possession proceedings on behalf of our client, Mrs Susan Reid, owner of 33 Willow Road, Enfield, EN2 6EA, against the tenant, Mr Mark Ellis. The tenant is in arrears in the sum of £5,300 as at 15 June 2024 and is also alleged to have sublet the premises without landlord consent, constituting a further breach of the tenancy agreement. Please commence proceedings on Grounds 8 and any applicable discretionary grounds. Enclosed are copies of the assured shorthold tenancy agreement, a rent statement evidencing arrears, correspondence with the tenant, witness statements from neighbours and photographic evidence of unauthorised occupation. Provide an estimate of costs, likely timeline and proposed next steps. Please confirm receipt of these instructions and advise if further documentation is required. This instruction is issued by Aisha Campbell of Campbell & Co acting as managing agent for Mrs Reid.

- Administrative requests: Confirm receipt of these instructions and advise whether any further documentation or information is required.

- Instruction provenance: Instruction issued by Aisha Campbell of Campbell & Co, acting as managing agent for Mrs Susan Reid.

Subject: Instruction to Commence Possession Proceedings

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I am writing to instruct you to commence possession proceedings on behalf of my client, Mrs Susan Reid, the owner of 33 Willow Road, Enfield, EN2 6EA, against the tenant, Mr Mark Ellis.

The tenancy in question is an Assured Shorthold Tenancy. As at 15 June 2024, Mr Ellis is in arrears of £5,300. Furthermore, we have reason to believe that he has breached the tenancy agreement by subletting the premises without the landlord's consent, constituting an additional breach.

We request that you commence proceedings on Ground 8 of the Housing Act 1988 and any applicable discretionary grounds. We have enclosed the necessary evidence and documentation, including:

* Correspondence with the tenant
* Witness statements from neighbours
* Photographic evidence of unauthorised occupation

Please confirm receipt of these

Best regards,

Subject: Proposal for Mediation and Resolution of Deposit Dispute

Dear [Tenant's Name] and [Landlord's Name],

I am writing to propose a fair mediation path to resolve the ongoing deposit dispute between you. The goal is to reach a mutually agreeable solution without escalating the matter further.

To facilitate this process, I kindly request that both parties submit evidence to support your respective claims. This evidence should include:

- Photos taken at the time of move-in and move-out
- The original inventory report
- Receipts for any cleaning services provided
- Receipts for any replacement items or repairs made

To ensure a smooth process, please note the following:

Let's aim to resolve this amicably. Please send photos and any receipts by Friday and we'll meet to review the evidence; if we can't agree we'll move to the deposit scheme adjudication.

I suggest we schedule a meeting to review the submitted evidence and work towards a resolution. I am available to attend the meeting and sit with the recipient if the parties would like. This will provide an opportunity for both parties to discuss their concerns and reach a mutually acceptable agreement.

If, after reviewing the evidence and discussing the matter, we are unable to reach an agreement, we will proceed to the deposit scheme

Subject: Update on Your Application and Next Steps

Dear [Applicant Name],

I wanted to personally reach out to you regarding the status of your application. I understand that the referencing process has taken a bit longer than anticipated, and for that, I apologize.

We are currently waiting on one employer reference, which typically takes up to five working days to be completed. I want to assure you that we are doing everything we can to expedite the process.

Dear Neighbor,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to touch base with you regarding the birdbath that's located near our shared fence. Lately, it's been attracting a lot of bees, and unfortunately, some of them have been entering my garden.

Best regards,
Aisha

general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly active voice with a mix of short, direct sentences for calls to action and medium-length compound sentences for descriptions and explanations. See you on the green,
Aisha

If you're considering making the Lea Valley your home, I'd be happy to show you the area's hidden gems and explain how this unique history has shaped the community we live in today.

task_instruction: Explain a 'subject to survey' clause to a first-time buyer
task_details: Buyer has signed an offer that is 'subject to survey'. Clause states: 'This offer is conditional on a satisfactory survey report within 14 days of exchange. Should the survey reveal major defects, the buyer may withdraw or renegotiate.' Explain what this means in plain English, stepwise, and give a clear example of how a discovered problem like subsidence would be handled. Reassure the buyer and suggest next steps.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, "subject to survey" means your offer is provisional until a surveyor checks the property and the report looks acceptable. First, you'll book a survey (I can recommend local surveyors). Then the surveyor inspects the house and writes up findings. If the report shows no big problems, the sale usually proceeds to exchange and completion as planned.

If the survey finds a serious issue, like subsidence (this means the ground beneath the house has moved), you have two main options. First option: you can withdraw your offer and get your deposit back, because the clause lets you pull out if the survey is unsatisfactory. Second option: you can try to renegotiate with the seller so the price is lowered or the seller pays for repairs — for example, if repairs are quoted at £12,000 you could ask the seller to reduce the price by that amount or offer a contribution towards repairs.

Practical next steps: book a RICS-qualified survey within the 14-day window. If the survey raises concerns, I’ll explain the report line by line and contact the seller’s agent to open talks. Happy to arrange the survey for you and walk through the report together — give me a bell when you’re ready.

All the best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Clarify a mortgage-approval clause for a buyer getting a mortgage
task_details: Offer includes a clause: 'Sale conditional on buyer obtaining mortgage offer within 21 days of exchange; if mortgage is not granted the buyer may withdraw and receive deposit back.' Explain what 'mortgage offer' and 'within 21 days' means, outline what happens if lender refuses, and advise what to do to minimise risk.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, the clause means the sale depends on your lender actually issuing a formal mortgage offer within 21 days of exchange. First, you apply for a mortgage and the lender does their checks. Then, if they approve, they send a mortgage offer document which confirms how much they will lend and on what terms (this is the mortgage offer).

If the lender refuses and you don’t get that offer within 21 days, the clause lets you withdraw from the purchase and get your deposit back. For example, if you applied for a £250,000 mortgage and the lender declines, you won’t be legally bound to proceed under that clause.

To reduce the chance of refusal, I’d recommend providing paperwork quickly — ID, payslips, bank statements — and keeping in regular contact with your mortgage broker. If the lender flags any issue, tell me straight away so we can look at alternatives. If you want, I can introduce a trusted local broker who's familiar with Enfield properties.

Speak soon,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a 'conditional upon sale of buyer's property' clause
task_details: Buyer's offer includes: 'This offer is conditional upon the sale of the buyer’s current property within 8 weeks of exchange. If the buyer's property does not exchange within this period the seller may cancel.' Explain the meaning, risks, and practical advice for a first-time buyer who doesn't have a property to sell but is being asked to include this clause.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, that clause means your purchase only goes ahead if your existing property sells within the stated 8 weeks. First, the seller wants certainty they aren’t left waiting indefinitely. Then, if your house doesn't exchange within eight weeks, the seller can pull out and sell to someone else.

For a first-time buyer who has no property to sell, you normally wouldn’t include this clause — it’s a clause for people who need the cash from one sale to buy another. If you’re being asked to include it, ask why; sometimes sellers request it when they already have another offer in the pipeline.

Risks: you could lose out if the seller prefers a buyer with no sale condition. Practical advice: explain you are chain-free (if true) and able to exchange and complete on the seller’s timeline. If you must agree to a condition, ask for a short time frame and agree terms that allow you to pull out if you can’t proceed. I can speak to the seller’s agent on your behalf to clarify their flexibility.

Happy to sort this with you over the phone.

Best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Break down a fixtures and fittings clause for a buyer
task_details: Clause reads: 'All fixtures and fittings are included except those specifically excluded in the attached inventory: chandelier in dining room, freestanding fridge, and personal items.' Explain what 'fixtures' and 'fittings' mean, how to interpret the inventory, and what to do if a disputed item is still in the property at completion.
personalized:
Hiya,

First, it’s about timing: until exchange of contracts the seller can legally negotiate with others. To protect yourself, aim to exchange as quickly as you can once your mortgage and searches are in order. Keep on top of paperwork with your solicitor and respond promptly to requests. If you can offer quicker exchange or a higher deposit, mention this to the seller to show you’re serious.

I’ll stay in close contact with the seller’s agent and push for realistic deadlines so we don’t lose the property. If you want, I’ll call your solicitor now and make sure nothing is holding us up.

Warmly,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a leasehold assignment clause about landlord consent
task_details: Clause reads: 'Assignment subject to landlord's consent which shall not be unreasonably withheld. Buyer must provide references within 14 days.' Explain what landlord consent means, typical reasons consent might be withheld, and what 'not unreasonably withheld' protects. Give a practical example.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, this clause means the lease is being transferred to you but the landlord must formally agree to that transfer. First, the landlord checks certain things — often references, proof of funds, and that you’ll use the property in the same way. Then they give consent in writing or refuse.

"Not unreasonably withheld" means the landlord can’t refuse for trivial or discriminatory reasons; they must have a sensible reason. Typical reasons for refusal might be poor references, evidence of previous rent arrears, or if your intended use breaches the lease (for example turning a family flat into an HMO without permission).

Example: you submit references and proof of deposit within 14 days; the landlord has no grounds to refuse and should give consent. If they try to refuse without a valid reason, we can push back and request clarification, and your solicitor can advise on remedies.

If you like, I’ll make sure we send everything the landlord needs straight away so that consent is smooth.

Best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a restrictive covenant clause to a buyer
task_details: Clause: 'Property subject to restrictive covenant preventing business use or external signage without prior written consent of the original developer.' Explain what a restrictive covenant is, how it affects use of the property, and what steps a buyer should take if they want to run a small home business or install a sign.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, a restrictive covenant is a rule attached to the land that limits what you can do with the property. First, read the covenant carefully: here it prevents running a business from the home or putting up external signs unless you get written permission from the original developer.

That means if you want to run a small home-based business (for example tutoring) or put a sign out front, you’ll need written consent. For small, low-impact home-working (using a laptop, meeting clients by appointment), many covenants are interpreted reasonably and consent is sometimes given. If your plans include regular customers visiting or external changes, you’ll probably need formal permission.

Practical steps: check how the covenant is worded in your legal pack, ask the seller’s solicitor whether any previous consents were granted, and if needed apply for consent early. If getting consent looks unlikely, consider whether the covenant affects your plans.

I’m happy to discuss your intended use and help approach the developer if you want.

Warm regards,
Aisha

All the best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a Section 106/planning obligation clause for extensions
task_details: Clause: 'Property subject to planning obligations (S106) restricting alterations that increase dwelling size beyond 25% or change number of units. Any breach may trigger repayment of grant.' Explain what S106 is, how this restriction affects ability to extend, and give an example of a permitted and non-permitted extension.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, Section 106 agreements are planning obligations attached to a property that set conditions on what you can do. First, this particular clause stops you increasing the house by more than 25% or changing how many separate homes are on the site without meeting the obligation.

That affects major extensions: a small single-storey rear extension that increases floor space by 10% would usually be fine, but adding a two-storey extension that increases the total area by 30% would breach the obligation and could lead to enforcement or financial penalties, such as repayment of a grant linked to the original development.

Example: a 15% rear kitchen extension is permitted. Building an extra flat above the existing house to create a new unit is not permitted without renegotiating the S106 terms with the council.

Practical step: if you’re thinking of extending, we’ll check the S106 wording and, if needed, discuss with the planning officer in Enfield to see what’s allowed or whether an application to vary the obligation is feasible.

Speak soon,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a deposit forfeiture clause if buyer withdraws late
task_details: Clause: 'If the buyer withdraws after exchange, deposit is forfeited to the seller, and seller reserves the right to claim further damages.' Explain what 'forfeited deposit' means, what 'damages' could be, and how a buyer can avoid this outcome with examples.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, once contracts are exchanged you’re legally committed. If you pull out after exchange, the deposit is likely lost — that’s what 'forfeited' means. First, the deposit (commonly 5–10% of the purchase price) will stay with the seller. Then, the seller can also seek extra compensation for losses they suffer if they can’t find another buyer quickly.

"Damages" might include the seller’s costs for re-marketing the property, any price reduction they had to accept, or legal fees. For example, if you exchanged on a £300,000 house with a £15,000 deposit and then withdraw, you lose the £15,000 and potentially face further claims if the seller sells for less later.

To avoid this, don’t exchange until you’re certain: ensure your mortgage is in place, searches are satisfactory, and you have a firm moving plan. If unexpected problems arise before exchange, negotiate a delay rather than a withdrawal.

If you’re worried about timings or risks, I’ll talk through safe milestones and help co-ordinate with your solicitor.

Kind regards,
Aisha

task_instruction: Clarify a clause about transfer of completion funds and timing
task_details: Clause: 'Buyer must ensure cleared funds are received by seller’s solicitors by 10am on completion date; any delay may incur interest at 4% above base rate.' Explain the meaning of cleared funds, the importance of timing, and what happens if bank transfers are delayed. Suggest practical steps to ensure funds arrive on time.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, the clause means your solicitor must get the money into the seller’s solicitor’s account in cleared funds by 10am on the agreed completion day. First, "cleared funds" means the money is fully available and not pending — a CHAPS transfer is usually required for same-day clearance.

If the payment is late, the seller can charge interest (for example base rate plus 4%). So, a late transfer could cost you extra money and might even delay completion, which causes stress for both parties.

Practical steps: instruct your solicitor to send a CHAPS on the morning of completion and confirm the exact beneficiary account. Tell your bank about the transfer in advance and check any limits. If your mortgage lender is sending money, confirm the time they will release funds and get a written confirmation from them.

I’ll remind both solicitors a few days before completion and can chase on the morning if needed.

Best wishes,
Aisha

Best,
Aisha

task_instruction: Explain a service charge apportionment clause in a leasehold purchase
task_details: Clause: 'Service charge payable proportionately; on completion seller pays up to completion date, buyer liable thereafter. Any apportionment disputes to be resolved between solicitors.' Explain how apportionment works, what the buyer can expect to pay immediately after completion, and how disputes are usually settled.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, service charges are costs for communal upkeep in flats, and apportionment means splitting the charge so the seller pays up to completion and you pay from completion onwards. First, your solicitor will ask for the latest service charge statement and check amounts due.

On completion you’ll normally take on liabilities from that date. If a service charge bill spans the completion date, it will be split pro rata — for example, if a £1,200 annual charge runs January–December and you complete on 1 July, the seller pays January–June and you pay July–December.

If there’s a disagreement about the correct split, solicitors try to resolve it quickly, often using the management company's records. It's uncommon for disputes to block completion; usually they sort out any small differences afterwards.

I’ll make sure your solicitor requests the latest service charge accounts and flags any unexpectedly large sums.

All the best,
Aisha

task_details: Clause: 'Buyer accepts property on an as-seen basis but seller confirms no knowledge of ground contamination. Explain what environmental searches cover, what contamination could mean, and how a buyer should respond if contamination is found.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, this clause says the seller isn’t aware of contamination but the property is sold as it stands. First, environmental searches look for things like former industrial use, fuel spills, or chemical contamination in the soil or groundwater. Then, if the search reveals contamination within 14 days you can withdraw under the clause.

Contamination can be costly to clean up and could affect future planning or mortgage availability. If a report shows an issue, you can ask for a full risk assessment and a remediation estimate. Depending on the findings you could withdraw, renegotiate the price, or require the seller to remediate before completion.

Practical step: instruct your solicitor to order an environmental search quickly and share the results with me. If anything worrying shows up, I’ll help you weigh up options and approach the seller.

Kind regards,
Aisha

task_details: Clause: 'Property may be subject to chancel repair liability; buyer advised to obtain a chancel search and indemnity if required.' Explain what chancel repair liability is, how likely it is in north London, and what an indemnity policy does with an example of potential costs.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, chancel repair liability is an old Church law that can require a property owner to pay for repairs to the local church chancel. First, it’s rare but can still exist where land was historically linked to a church. In north London it’s uncommon but not impossible, depending on the parish history.

An indemnity policy protects you financially if a claim is later made. For example, if a historic claim asked for £20,000 and you had an indemnity policy, the insurer would cover the cost instead of you paying out.

Practical step: get a chancel search in the conveyancing stage; if it flags a risk we usually buy an indemnity policy for a modest one-off premium rather than delaying exchange.

If you’d like, I’ll ask your solicitor to include this search immediately.

Best regards,
Aisha

personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, a Tree Preservation Order (TPO) protects specific trees so you can’t cut them down or do major work without council permission. First, check which trees the TPO covers — that will be detailed in the title documents or the council records. Then, even pruning can require notification or consent depending on the work.

If you want to prune or remove a tree, you apply to Enfield Council with a plan and reason. The council assesses the impact; if you do work without permission you can be fined and may be ordered to replace the tree. For example, removing a large protected maple without consent could lead to a substantial fine and mandatory replanting.

Practical advice: get the tree schedule from your solicitor and, if you plan changes, consult an arborist and make a formal application before doing anything.

All the best,
Aisha

Aisha

If you find such an issue, gather the documentary evidence and tell your solicitor immediately so they can raise it with the seller and seek a fair adjustment.

I’ll always check adverts and the title documents for consistency, and if anything looks off we’ll pause and confirm before you commit.

Kind regards,
Aisha
